title: Checkpoint: Plates, Quakes and Volcanoes
objective: After this level you can explain what a plate boundary, fault or hotspot means for the quakes and eruptions a place can expect.
summary: A place's plate setting predicts its hazards: subduction zones bring the largest quakes and explosive volcanoes, rifts and transform faults bring their own quakes, and hotspots build lines of shields.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: read a place's dangers from its plate setting.
cards.body: Show a geologist where a town sits on the plate map, and she can tell you a lot about the quakes and eruptions it should prepare for. After nine levels, so can you.

cards.headline: Subduction: the biggest of both
cards.body: Where one plate dives beneath another, both hazards peak. The world's largest earthquakes, magnitude 9 and above, happen in subduction zones. And subduction feeds volcanoes like the Cascades, from southern British Columbia to northern California. Their high-silica magma is thick and pasty and traps gas, so they can erupt explosively. One diving plate, two dangers.

mascot.line: This is Levels 12, 16 and 18 working together. If you can explain why subduction zones are so dangerous, you've got the chapter.

items.label: Pulling apart
points: Normal faults as the crust stretches

items.label: Sliding past
points: Strike-slip faults like the San Andreas
Locked sections store strain for great quakes

items.label: Over a hotspot
points: A chain of volcanoes, older with distance
Fluid basalt builds shields like Mauna Loa

cards.headline: Then check the ground
cards.body: Whatever the setting, the ground under a town matters too. A quake has one magnitude but many intensities: shaking fades with distance from the rupture, and soft mud shakes far more than bedrock. Two neighbors on the same plate boundary can have very different days.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: How a place's plate setting tells you which quakes and volcanoes to expect there.
Why subduction zones make both the largest earthquakes and the most explosive volcanoes.
How a locked fault stores strain in bent rock and releases it as an earthquake.
Why runny basalt builds gentle shields while sticky, gassy magma builds steep, explosive cones.

questions.prompt: Plates, Quakes and Volcanoes recap: where do the world's largest earthquakes happen?

options.label: Along creeping faults
options.rationale: Creeping sections have only small quakes.

options.label: At divergent rifts like Iceland's
options.rationale: The largest, M 9 and up, are in subduction zones.

questions.explanation: The world's largest earthquakes, magnitude 9 and above, occur in subduction zones.

questions.prompt: Plates, Quakes and Volcanoes recap: why can Cascade volcanoes erupt explosively?

options.label: Their magma is runny basalt that sprays out
They sit over a hotspot in the middle of a plate
options.rationale: They sit above a subduction zone.

options.label: Their silica-rich magma is thick and traps gas
They erupt under the sea, where water boils
options.rationale: They are on land, fed by subduction.

questions.explanation: Subduction feeds the Cascades with high-silica magma, which is thick and pasty and traps gas until it bursts out.

questions.prompt: Plates, Quakes and Volcanoes recap: what is released when a locked fault suddenly slips?

options.label: Magma stored under the fault
options.rationale: Locked faults store strain, not magma.

options.label: Heat from radioactive decay
options.rationale: That heats the interior; it doesn't set off quakes directly.

options.label: Water trapped in the soil
options.rationale: That's part of liquefaction, not the quake itself.

questions.explanation: While a fault is locked, bent rock stores strain; when the fault slips, the rock snaps back and releases it as an earthquake.

questions.prompt: Plates, Quakes and Volcanoes recap: why does a hotspot leave a whole line of volcanoes instead of one?

options.label: The hotspot erupts in a new random spot each time
options.rationale: The line has a clear age order.

options.label: The plate moves over a hotspot that stays roughly put
Earthquakes crack the plate into a straight line
options.rationale: The line comes from plate motion over the hotspot.

questions.explanation: A plate carries each volcano away from the hotspot, so new ones keep forming and old ones trail behind.

questions.prompt: Plates, Quakes and Volcanoes recap: two towns feel the same quake. Which one probably shakes harder?

options.label: The one on bedrock, far from the rupture
options.rationale: Distance and bedrock both lower the shaking.

options.label: The one on soft mud, close to the rupture
Neither: one magnitude means equal shaking

questions.explanation: Shaking depends mostly on distance from the rupture, and soft mud shakes more than bedrock.
